A '''stadium''' is a two-dimensional [[geometric shape]] constructed of a [[rectangle]] with [[semicircle]]s at a pair of opposite sides.<ref>{{mathworld|id=Stadium|title=Stadium}}</ref>
The same shape is known also as a '''pill shape''',<ref>{{cite journal
 | last1 = O'Hara | first1 = Michael J.
 | last2 = O'Leary | first2 = Dianne P.
 | date = April 2008
 | doi = 10.1103/physreva.77.042319
 | issue = 4
 | journal = Physical Review A
 | pages = 042319-1 – 042319-20
 | publisher = American Physical Society (APS)
 | title = Adiabatic theorem in the presence of noise
 | volume = 77| arxiv = 0801.3872
 }}</ref> '''discorectangle''',<ref>{{cite journal|last=Dzubiella|first=Joachim|author2=Matthias Schmidt|author3-link=Hartmut Löwen|author3=Hartmut Löwen |title=Topological defects in nematic droplets of hard spherocylinders|journal=Physical Review E|year=2000|volume=62|issue=4 |pages=5081–5091 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevE.62.5081|pmid=11089056 |arxiv=cond-mat/9906388|bibcode=2000PhRvE..62.5081D|s2cid=31381033 }}</ref> '''obround''',<ref>{{Cite web|url = http://www.vista-industrial.com/obround.php|title = Obround - Punching Tools - VIP, Inc.|last = Ackermann|first = Kurt|website = www.vista-industrial.com|access-date = 2016-04-29}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url = http://www.ljstar.com/Products/industrial-sight-glass-obround-level-gauges|title = Obround Level Gauge Glass : L.J. Star Incorporated|website = L.J.Star Incorporated|language = en-US|access-date = 2016-04-29|url-status = dead|archiveurl = https://web.archive.org/web/20160422090036/http://www.ljstar.com/products/industrial-sight-glass-obround-level-gauges/|archivedate = 2016-04-22}}</ref> '''racetrack''' or '''sausage body'''.<ref name=sausage>{{cite journal|last1=Huang|first1=Pingliang|last2=Pan|first2=Shengliang|last3=Yang|first3=Yunlong|doi=10.1007/s00454-015-9715-9|doi-access=|issue=3|journal=[[Discrete & Computational Geometry]]|mr=3392976|pages=728–740|title=Positive center sets of convex curves|volume=54|year=2015}}</ref>

The shape is based on a [[stadium]], a place used for [[athletics track|athletics]] and [[horse racing]] tracks.

A stadium may be constructed as the [[Minkowski sum]] of a [[Disk (mathematics)|disk]] and a [[line segment]].<ref name=sausage/> Alternatively, it is the [[neighborhood (mathematics)|neighborhood]] of points within a given distance from a line segment.
A stadium is a type of [[oval]]. However, unlike some other ovals such as the [[ellipse]]s, it is not an [[algebraic curve]] because  different parts of its boundary are defined by different equations.

== Formulas ==
The [[perimeter]] of a stadium is calculated by the formula <math>P = 2 (\pi r+a)</math> where  ''a'' is the length of the straight sides and ''r'' is the radius of the semicircles. With the same parameters, the [[area (geometry)|area]] of the stadium is <math>A = \pi r^2 + 2ra = r(\pi r + 2a)</math>.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.calculatorsoup.com/calculators/geometry-plane/stadium.php |title=Stadium Calculator |publisher=Calculatorsoup.com |accessdate=2013-01-31}}</ref>

==Bunimovich stadium==
When this shape is used in the study of [[dynamical billiards]], it is called the [[Bunimovich stadium]]. [[Leonid Bunimovich]] used this shape to show that it is possible for billiard tracks to exhibit [[chaos theory|chaotic behavior]] (positive [[Lyapunov exponent]] and exponential divergence of paths) even within a convex billiard table.<ref>{{cite journal|last=Bunimovič|first=L. A.|authorlink=Leonid Bunimovich|issue=3|journal=Funkcional. Anal. I Priložen.|mr=0357736|pages=73–74|title=The ergodic properties of certain billiards|volume=8|year=1974}}</ref>

==Related shapes==
A ''[[Capsule (geometry)|capsule]]'' is produced by revolving a stadium around the [[line of symmetry]] that [[Bisection|bisects]] the semicircles.
